transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose I'm here because of my job. I'm a translator, and for months now, I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern in our project files. Certain subcontractors and this one colleague of mine keep making these tiny changes to the translation memory and the timestamps, just to make it look like my quality control failed. It's incredibly frustrating. 

I actually started out doing live interpretation, though—mostly French and Arabic. Arabic is such a fascinating language, the root system is just so logical. You take three consonants and you can build a whole web of meaning
Aside from noticing these changes in your files, have you ever heard voices or sounds, or seen things that other people around you don't seem to notice?

No, no, nothing like that. I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. I mean, my hearing is extremely sensitive, but that's just because of my training. In simultaneous interpretation, you have to listen to the speaker and talk at the exact same time, so your ears get tuned to every little sound. 

I remember this one conference in Brussels a few years ago... the headsets they gave us were just awful. There was this constant static hiss in the left earpiece. I complained to the organizers because, honestly, how are you supposed to catch the nuances of a Maghrebi accent through static? Regional dialects are tricky enough as it is. Like, the way they pronounce certain guttural sounds in North Africa versus the Levant... it's a completely different placement in the throat, and if the audio is bad and you miss it, you could mistranslate the whole concept for the delegates. It's a huge responsibility. 

But anyway, no, I don't hear... you know, imaginary things. Just bad audio equipment sometimes.
Outside of this situation at work, do you find yourself generally suspicious or distrustful of other people in your life—like friends, family, or neighbors—doubting their loyalty or motives?

No, I don't... I don't doubt my family or my neighbors or anything like that. Outside of this whole project issue, my life is completely normal. I still do my own translations, manage my team’s workflow, pay the bills, keep up with all the usual family routines. The only place things really go off track is when the file history or those certain coworkers come up. It's just that specific situation. 

But yeah, family routines... my wife and I actually just started taking our dog to this new agility training class on Saturday mornings. Have you ever seen those competitions? It's really fascinating. It's almost like a form of cross-species interpreting, when you think about it. You have to be so precise with your body language and hand signals, because if you drop your wrist even a fraction of an inch, the dog takes the wrong tunnel or misses a jump completely. We had this instructor last week who used to train search and rescue dogs in the Alps, and he was telling us how the dogs actually read the micro-expressions on your face before you even give the verbal command. Just incredible animals. I've been reading this book he recommended about canine cognition and how their olfactory cortex maps to memory... 

But anyway, what were we... oh, right. No, no issues with my friends or family. They're fine.

Have you had similar experiences of feeling that people were deliberately undermining or deceiving you at other points earlier in your life, or is this the first time in your life you've felt this way?

No, honestly, this is the first time. I've never had a problem like this before. I mean, I've worked with some difficult people, sure, but nobody who went out of their way to sabotage the translation memory like this. Usually, translators are a pretty collaborative bunch. 

Actually, collaboration is so important in this field, especially when you're dealing with localization. You know, making sure a phrase works culturally in the target language. I was working on this manual for a medical device company once, and they wanted to use this idiom that made perfect sense in English but in Japanese, it sounded completely absurd. The Japanese translator and I spent hours going back and forth over email trying to find the right cultural equivalent. It's fascinating how culture shapes language, isn't it? Like how some indigenous languages don't have words for left and right, they use absolute cardinal directions instead. So you'd say, "There's an ant on your southwest leg." Can you imagine having to orient yourself to a compass just to speak? It really changes how your brain maps space. 

But, uh, anyway... no, this kind of deliberate tampering? First time. It's just so bizarre.
How long has it been since you first started noticing this pattern with the file changes—when did it begin?

Let's see... it's been going on for about 11 months now. Yeah, it started shortly after I was put in charge of the new localization project. It was a massive rollout for a client in the agricultural tech sector, which, let me tell you, agricultural terminology is an absolute nightmare to translate. The equipment names are so hyper-specific. Like, a combine harvester has all these different internal parts—the threshing drum, the straw walkers, the chaffer... I had to spend three days just reading up on tractor manuals to understand how a grain tank unloader works in German. 

My uncle actually used to own a small farm in Ohio when I was a kid. We'd go visit in the summers, and he had this old red tractor, a Massey Ferguson, I think. We used to ride on the back while he baled hay. The smell of fresh-cut alfalfa is just... there's nothing quite like it. It really stays with you, you know? Olfactory memory is the strongest trigger for nostalgia, just like that book I was telling you about with the dogs. Anyway, he ended up selling the farm to a commercial developer back in the nineties, which was a shame, really. They just paved over the whole thing and put up a strip mall with a mattress store and a frozen yogurt place. 

But, um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the timeline. Yeah, about 11 months ago is when the tampering started.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a single, well-systematized, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (belief that coworkers are deliberately tampering with translation files to sabotage his work quality) persisting for approximately 11 months. He denies hallucinations (auditory or visual), and his affect, behavior, and functioning remain intact and unimpaired outside the delusional theme—he continues working, managing his team, maintaining family routines, and engaging in hobbies. There is no evidence of prior episodes of suspiciousness, no pervasive distrust of family/friends/neighbors, and no negative symptoms, disorganized behavior, or broader psychotic symptoms suggestive of schizophrenia. The circumstantial, tangential speech noted is more consistent with personality style/rambling rather than formal thought disorder, and does not meet threshold for disorganized speech criteria. The encapsulated nature of the delusion, preserved functioning, and absence of hallucinations or other psychotic domains support Delusional Disorder, Persecutory Type (F22) over Schizophrenia (F20.0). Paranoid Personality Disorder (F60.0) was considered but ruled out given the fixed, delusional (not merely characterological) quality of the belief and lack of pervasive interpersonal distrust across life domains.
